content: To ensure effective data management and budgeting, a schedule for sampling cases should be established, considering logistical factors, climatic conditions, and laboratory workload. All laboratory methods and quality assurance systems must be discussed and agreed upon with the partner Supra-National Reference Laboratory (SRL). The protocol should also address ethical considerations and account for the time required to obtain necessary approvals from ethical review panels. The development of the protocol must involve both an experienced epidemiologist and a statistician. A checklist for survey protocol development is provided in Annex 2. The World Health Organization (WHO) and other technical partners can assist in the development and review of the survey protocol before its implementation. This ensures that all requirements are comprehensively addressed, quality control measures are in place, and the data collected is representative of the geographically defined population under study. Once finalized, the protocol should be distributed to all coordination team members and health staff involved in the survey. A Central Reference Laboratory, typically the National Reference Laboratory, should be linked to all intermediate tuberculosis (TB) laboratories and the majority of TB diagnostic centers. If a quality-assured central laboratory is not available, sputum specimens may need to be shipped to an external laboratory. Diagnostic and treatment centers should sample patients from institutions where individuals suspected of having TB are registered. These institutions are often non-specialized health centers or outpatient departments of hospitals operated by the government or non-governmental organizations. The roles of all relevant healthcare providers, including public, voluntary, private, and corporate entities not formally linked to the national TB control program, should be carefully considered in the diagnosis and treatment of TB. Including care providers outside the national control program requires particular attention to maintaining quality standards in diagnostics, sampling, data recording, and reporting. Countries with a significant private healthcare sector should aim to include private health centers in the survey to obtain results representative of the entire TB patient population. Public-private mix initiatives can serve as platforms to gradually involve private-sector laboratories in drug resistance surveillance activities. Quality-assured microscopy, along with adequate referral systems for molecular testing and/or culture and drug susceptibility testing (DST), are prerequisites for implementing a drug resistance survey. The Central Reference Laboratory is responsible for identifying Mycobacterium tuberculosis and performing DST using molecular or culture-based methods. It also ensures the quality of smear microscopy, molecular testing, and culture and DST performed by regional or peripheral units through regular on-site supervision and training in laboratory procedures and quality assurance systems. An external quality assessment program with a partner SRL validates the results of susceptibility tests conducted by the Central Reference Laboratory and other relevant laboratories. Basic laboratory equipment and materials must be available and functional in the Central Reference Laboratory before implementing a survey. Drug resistance surveys should only be conducted when laboratories meet appropriate biosafety standards and are equipped with trained staff following clear standard operating procedures and producing quality-assured data. It is important to note that drug resistance surveys significantly increase the workload of the reference laboratory and should only be undertaken where capacity is sufficient. Statistical methodology is a fundamental aspect of survey design, and an experienced epidemiologist or statistician should be involved from the early planning stages. The sampling frame for a survey depends on its objectives and the testing methods to be used. For example, to measure the proportion of new cases with anti-tuberculosis drug resistance using culture-based methods, the sampling frame should include all new sputum smear-positive pulmonary TB patients in the study area. Continuous surveillance of drug resistance among previously treated patients should be a priority in all countries, as it provides crucial information for program management. In settings where routine DST for previously treated cases is not yet in place, a separate sample size calculation should ideally be devised for a survey of these patients. However, due to the small number of previously treated patients notified annually, achieving this sample size may not be feasible. Instead, during the survey enrollment period for new patients, all previously treated patients presenting to study sites should be enrolled. Estimates in previously treated cases are likely to be less precise than those in new cases, and analysis of subcategories may not be possible. Culture-based surveys are typically based on sputum smear-positive TB cases for two reasons: (1) there is no strong evidence to suggest that the proportion of drug-resistant cases varies significantly between smear-positive and smear-negative TB cases, and (2) the culture yield from smear-negative patients is relatively low compared to smear-positive cases and is more negatively affected by delays in sputum transport. Including cases with a low culture yield requires a significantly larger sample size and may increase laboratory workload up to tenfold. Countries interested in including sputum smear-negative cases should carefully consider the logistical and laboratory capacity implications. If molecular technologies such as Xpert MTB/RIF are used, the sampling frame could be expanded to include patients with presumptive TB, regardless of smear microscopy results. In this case, all patients with presumptive TB must be tested instead of only those prioritized by national testing guidelines. Calculating an appropriate sample size can be challenging, as information about the number of patients with presumptive TB is often not centrally available. Since less TB is found among smear-negative presumptive TB patients than among smear-positive patients, a greater number of patients will need to be tested, resulting in a much higher demand for resources. If a survey aims to determine the relative risk of drug-resistant TB among HIV-positive TB patients compared with HIV-negative TB patients, a more complex study design with a larger sample size would be required. Few countries have conducted such studies, so it is important to seek appropriate technical support for advice on survey design and laboratory needs when designing such a protocol. For surveys measuring the proportion of new cases with multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB), the calculation of an appropriate sample size should consider the total number of new sputum smear-positive pulmonary cases registered in the previous year in the study area, the expected proportion of new cases with MDR-TB based on available data, and the desired precision of the estimate, expressed as a confidence interval of at least 95%. Sampling uncertainty should be minimized while ensuring the calculated sample size is logistically feasible. If cluster sampling is adopted, the correlation between individuals within a cluster must be accounted for, and a design effect of 2 should be assumed unless estimated from previous surveys. The calculated sample size must be adjusted to account for potential losses, such as patients who do not consent to participate, provide inadequate samples, or whose samples are contaminated or yield uninterpretable results. For culture-based surveys, a loss of 10-15% should be incorporated into the sample size calculation; for molecular-based surveys, 5-10% is appropriate. Countries repeating a survey should aim to document differences in the proportion of drug-resistant cases compared to previous surveys. The sample size should be calculated to detect a significant difference between the proportions of MDR-TB found in the previous and current surveys. Different sampling strategies can be adopted to select a representative sample of TB patients. Randomization is essential to select a representative group of newly registered patients, but simple random sampling within health centers is rarely feasible due to potential disruption of routine activities. Randomization can occur at the health center or district level, ensuring routine activities are minimally affected. Cluster sampling methods are best used in settings where it is logistically difficult to cover the entire country and where the number of health centers registering TB patients is high. A minimum of 30 clusters is recommended, with cluster sizes between 10 and 40 patients to ensure clusters are neither too small nor too large.
